reserves.name: IMPERIAL GREEN LONGPOD (green)
reserves.text: Tall, green-seeded broad bean with long pods, suitable for a main crop.

reserves.name: BUNYARD'S EXHIBITION (white)
reserves.text: Traditional longpod broad bean with white seeds, suitable for cooking fresh or freezing.

reserves.name: EXPRESS (greenish white)
reserves.text: One of the fastest maturing of all broad beans - choose it if you intend to sow in early spring. Has earned a high reputation as a heavy cropper.

reserves.name: RELON (green)
reserves.text: A giant among broad beans - pod lengths over 20 in. with 10 beans per pod are claimed. Good for freezing - even better for the show bench.

reserves.name: IMPERIAL WHITE LONGPOD (white)
reserves.text: White-seeded longpod broad bean for kitchen or exhibition use.

reserves.name: HYLON (white)
reserves.text: White-seeded broad bean grown for its long pods.

reserves.name: WITKIEM VROMA (white)
reserves.text: The Witkiem varieties are for sowing in early spring and for picking with the autumn-sown types.

reserves.name: RED EPICURE (reddish brown)
reserves.text: Quite, quite different to any other variety - the red beans turn yellow when cooked. The flavour is distinctive.

reserves.name: GREEN WINDSOR (green)
reserves.text: Green-seeded Windsor broad bean with broad pods and good flavour.

reserves.name: JUBILEE HYSOR (white)
reserves.text: White-seeded Windsor type with broad pods. Suited to spring sowing and a later crop.

reserves.name: BONNY LAD (white)
reserves.text: Not much to choose between this variety and The Sutton, but it does grow rather taller (15-18 in. compared to 12 in.) and the beans are white-eyed.

varieties.name: Blue Lake White Seeded
varieties.text: Climbing bean for tender green pods or dried white haricots. Let some pods mature and dry for winter.

varieties.name: Cobra
varieties.text: Slender green pods and a long picking season. Give climbers sturdy supports and pick regularly.

varieties.name: Tendergreen
varieties.text: Traditional dwarf with green pods, useful where tall supports will not fit.

varieties.name: Algarve
varieties.text: Vigorous climber with broad, flat green pods, contrasting with pencil-podded types.

varieties.name: Purple Teepee (purple)
varieties.text: Dwarf with easily seen purple pods, which turn green when cooked. Suits compact beds.

reserves.name: HUNTER
reserves.text: The pods are long, wide, straight and stringless - this high-yielding climber is widely available.

reserves.name: THE PRINCE
reserves.text: Aptly named - the most popular of all french bean varieties. It is a dwarf-growing Flat-pod which is recommended for exhibition.

reserves.name: MASTERPIECE
reserves.text: Another old favourite Flat-pod - suitable for early sowing. An excellent general-purpose bean, say the experts.

reserves.name: CANADIAN WONDER
reserves.text: A heavy cropping Flat-pod - once popular but no longer to be found in all the catalogues.

reserves.name: PURPLE QUEEN (purple)
reserves.text: A purple-podded French bean whose pods turn dark green when cooked. Valued for flavour and high yields.

reserves.name: BLAUHILDE (purple)
reserves.text: A decorative climber with purple flowers and purple beans, useful for easy picking and a long harvest.

reserves.name: BORLOTTO LINGUA DI FUOCO
reserves.text: A climbing bean with red-and-cream striped pods. Pick young pods as flat beans or let them mature for dried beans.

reserves.name: ANNABEL
reserves.text: A compact variety which bears masses of thin stringless pods. It is a good choice if you want to grow french beans in pots or growing bags.

reserves.name: LOCH NESS
reserves.text: A stringless Pencil-pod which will withstand colder conditions than other varieties.

reserves.name: CROPPER TEEPEE
reserves.text: The Pencil-pods are large with white seeds - a reliable heavy-cropping variety with good disease resistance.

reserves.name: NASSAU
reserves.text: A stringless Flat-pod with a good reputation for high quality flavour and easy picking. The pods reach 6 in. or more.

reserves.name: MASAI
reserves.text: This is one of the Kenyan varieties - the short 'filet' pods are very narrow and can be cooked whole.

reserves.name: PROS
reserves.text: A truly continental bean - round, narrow and stringless.

reserves.name: CHEVRIER VERT
reserves.text: The most popular haricot variety, which you will find in some but not all catalogues. You can cook them at the flageolet stage or allow them to dry as cream-coloured haricot beans.

reserves.name: CUPIDON
reserves.text: A high-yielding dwarf bean with long, tender green pods and a long picking season.

reserves.name: HELDA
reserves.text: An early, flat-podded climbing bean with a relatively short harvest period, useful for a quick crop from a supported row.

reserves.name: WESTLANDSE
reserves.text: A productive climber giving repeated harvests of round green beans over a medium season.

reserves.name: MONT D'OR (yellow)
reserves.text: The 6-in. round pods have a waxy flesh and contain black seeds. Cook whole - considered by many to be the best of the Waxpods.

reserves.name: KINGHORN WAX (yellow)
reserves.text: A stringless Waxpod renowned for its flavour. The flesh is creamy yellow.

reserves.name: PURPLE-PODDED CLIMBING (purple)
reserves.text: Grows about 5 ft high. Decorative with its pendent bunches of dark purple beans which turn green when cooked.

reserves.name: SONESTA (yellow)
reserves.text: A fast-cropping dwarf waxpod with yellow pods that are easy to spot among the leaves and a slightly waxy taste.

varieties.name: Moonlight
varieties.text: White-flowered runner–French cross with reliable pod set and tender green pods.

varieties.name: Firestorm
varieties.text: Red-flowered runner–French cross for reliable cropping on a bean frame.

varieties.name: Enorma
varieties.text: Traditional long-podded runner for tall supports; long, straight beans.

varieties.name: White Lady
varieties.text: White-flowered climber with long, tender pods. Pick young and often.

varieties.name: Pickwick
varieties.text: Dwarf runner for containers and small plots, with less yield than a full-height frame.

reserves.name: POLESTAR
reserves.text: Red flowers produce a heavy yield of top quality stringless pods. The cropping season is long and it remains one of the best all-round choices.

reserves.name: ACHIEVEMENT
reserves.text: Long straight pods, making it a good exhibition variety. Recommended for freezing.

reserves.name: STREAMLINE
reserves.text: Traditional climbing runner bean. Pick young pods regularly for a long cropping season.

reserves.name: SCARLET EMPEROR
reserves.text: A popular all-round performer - long, straight beans which are produced earlier than the maincrop.

reserves.name: PAINTED LADY
reserves.text: Well-named - the white-faced flowers have bright red lips. The pods are relatively short, but it is an attractive plant for using as a screen.

reserves.name: LADY DI
reserves.text: Red-flowered climber with long, stringless pods. Keep roots moist from flowering onwards.

reserves.name: HESTIA
reserves.text: A dwarf runner bean suitable for pots and small spaces. It has a shorter season than climbing varieties, so sow more than once if a longer crop is wanted.

reserves.name: RED KNIGHT
reserves.text: Red-flowered runner bean with stringless pods, suitable for freezing.

reserves.name: MERGOLES
reserves.text: White flowers, white seeds and stringless pods. An excellent choice for kitchen use - sets well, freezes well and crops over a long period. Your seed catalogue may offer Desiree instead - there is not a great deal of difference.

reserves.name: DESIREE
reserves.text: White seeds in stringless narrow pods, freezes well - a good choice.

reserves.name: KELVEDON MARVEL
reserves.text: An early cropper, producing its rather short pods about 14 days before the standard varieties.

reserves.name: SUNSET
reserves.text: Salmon-pink flowers. A climbing runner with green pods; provide supports and keep roots moist during flowering to encourage pod set.

reserves.name: CRUSADER
reserves.text: Often called the 'exhibitor's runner bean' because of the outstanding length of its pods.

reserves.name: CZAR
reserves.text: A white-flowered variety often grown for dried white butter beans. Do not keep picking it for green pods if the aim is a dry autumn harvest; let pods mature and dry for winter storage.

reserves.name: HAMMOND'S DWARF SCARLET
reserves.text: The popular red-flowering form which is early maturing and will continue to crop for many weeks if picked regularly. No support.

varieties.name: Bright Lights
varieties.text: A colourful chard selection with stems in several shades. Harvest young leaves for salads or larger leaves and stems for cooking.

varieties.name: Rhubarb Chard
varieties.text: Red stalks and dark leaves make this chard decorative as well as useful. Treat it as a red-stemmed type unless a cultivar is specified.

varieties.name: Spinach Beet
varieties.text: A leaf beet grown for repeated picking of green leaves. Useful as a cooking green through a longer season than true spinach.

varieties.name: Fordhook Giant
varieties.text: A white-stemmed chard with broad green leaves. A useful kitchen choice when leaf yield matters more than mixed stem colours.

reserves.name: SWISS CHARD
reserves.text: Also known as seakale beet or silver chard. It produces deep narrow roots rather than a swollen beetroot and is grown for broad leaves and thick edible midribs. White-stemmed types such as Lucullus, Fordhook Giant and White-Silver 2 are sometimes listed.

reserves.name: RAINBOW CHARD
reserves.text: A colourful strain of Swiss chard with stems in shades of red, yellow, white and pink. It is ornamental in the garden and useful in the kitchen, but still needs regular picking while the leaves are tender.

varieties.name: Boltardy
varieties.text: A familiar round red beetroot valued for resistance to bolting. A useful choice for earlier sowings under suitable conditions.

varieties.name: Pablo F1
varieties.text: A round red beetroot producing uniform roots with good kitchen quality. Harvest young for tender roots.

varieties.name: Cylindra
varieties.text: Long, cylindrical red roots make even slices easy. Useful for cooking and pickling when shape matters more than round presentation.

varieties.name: Chioggia
varieties.text: A heritage beetroot with pink-and-white rings when cut raw. Grow for visual variety alongside a standard red beetroot.

varieties.name: Forono
varieties.text: An elongated red beetroot with a tidy shape for slicing. Retain as an established alternative to round-rooted selections.

reserves.name: CHELTENHAM GREEN TOP
reserves.text: Long, sweet roots for autumn use and winter storage. Grow in deep, friable soil and lift sound roots before hard frost.

reserves.name: DETROIT 2
reserves.text: With the older Detroit it is the standard Globe variety for later planting. Renowned for its flavour.
reserves.short_text: With the older Detroit it is the standard Globe variety for later planting. Renowned for its flavour.

reserves.name: MONOPOLY
reserves.text: Bolt-resistant like Boltardy with the added advantage of being a monogerm variety (one seedling per 'seed').
reserves.short_text: Bolt-resistant like Boltardy with the added advantage of being a monogerm variety (one seedling per 'seed').

reserves.name: DETROIT 2-LITTLE BALL
reserves.text: The favourite choice for late sowing. Produces 'baby' beets which are excellent for pickling and bottling.
reserves.short_text: The favourite choice for late sowing. Produces 'baby' beets which are excellent for pickling and bottling.

reserves.name: DETROIT 2-NEW GLOBE
reserves.text: A good choice for the show bench. The shape is uniform, the texture is good and the flesh is free from rings.
reserves.short_text: A good choice for the show bench. The shape is uniform, the texture is good and the flesh is free from rings.

reserves.name: BURPEE'S GOLDEN
reserves.text: Orange skin and sweet yellow flesh that does not bleed into other foods. Also known as Golden Detroit; useful for salads and mixed dishes.
reserves.short_text: Orange skin and sweet yellow flesh that does not bleed into other foods. Also known as Golden Detroit; useful for salads and mixed dishes.

reserves.name: ALBINA VEREDUNA
reserves.text: The most popular white variety - sometimes sold as Snowhite. Not widely available like Burpee's Golden or the popular reds, but well worth looking for. The flavour is excellent and the leaves can be cooked as 'greens', but it does not store well.

varieties.name: Early Purple Sprouting
varieties.text: An overwintering broccoli producing purple shoots in spring. Allow it a long growing season and pick the shoots regularly.

varieties.name: Green Magic F1
varieties.text: An early calabrese producing a dense central head followed by side shoots. A practical choice for a summer broccoli crop.

varieties.name: Claret F1
varieties.text: A purple-sprouting broccoli for a later spring harvest. Useful for extending cropping beyond earlier sprouting varieties.

varieties.name: Marathon F1
varieties.text: A dependable summer calabrese with firm blue-green heads. A useful alternative to Green Magic for the main crop.

varieties.name: Early Purple Sprouting

reserves.name: WHITE EYE
reserves.text: A white sprouting type grown for pale spring spears. White sprouting broccoli is generally a spring crop rather than an autumn crop.

reserves.name: GREEN SPROUTING
reserves.text: An open-pollinated type useful for smaller but more repeated harvests rather than one large head.

reserves.name: NINE STAR PERENNIAL
reserves.text: A short-lived perennial with a pale central head and smaller side heads. Harvest before flowering; plants may crop for three or four years.

reserves.name: RED ARROW
reserves.text: A purple sprouting variety for spring picking. Harvest firm, unopened spears regularly.

reserves.name: LATE PURPLE SPROUTING
reserves.text: A late spring-cropping type, often ready in April. Plants can reach about 3 ft tall.

reserves.name: EARLY WHITE SPROUTING
reserves.text: The one to grow if you want to cut the crop in March and early April.

reserves.name: LATE WHITE SPROUTING
reserves.text: Extends the harvesting period for broccoli lovers - spears appear in April and early May.

reserves.name: EXPRESS CORONA
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid - one of the earliest of all the green sprouting types. About 45 days after planting out the central head is ready for cutting - side shoots then freely develop to give a succession of succulent spears.

reserves.name: GREEN COMET
reserves.text: An early F1 hybrid with a large central head. Heads can be about 7 in. across and weigh around 1 lb; side-shoot production is limited.

reserves.name: CORVETTE
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid which matures in about 60 days after transplanting. It gives you the best of both worlds - the primary head is large and firm, but after its removal there is a succession of secondary spears.

reserves.name: ITALIAN SPROUTING
reserves.text: This is the basic variety which has kept its place in some catalogues despite the appearance of modern F1 hybrids. It has an excellent reputation for flavour and a long cropping season.

reserves.name: SHOGUN
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid which bears large blue-green heads with many lateral shoots below them. It is tolerant of cold conditions and a wide range of soil types. Early maturing - good for freezing.

reserves.name: BELSTAR F1
reserves.text: A useful F1 calabrese for early heads and autumn cropping; suitable where a single large head followed by smaller shoots is wanted.

reserves.name: PURPLE SPROUTING
reserves.text: Sometimes the seed packet does not tell you whether it is 'Early' or 'Late'. You will find that the spears appear in March and April.

reserves.name: ROMANESCO
reserves.text: A cauliflower type with green, pointed florets. Retained here as a related crop; follow cauliflower guidance and the named selection’s harvest dates.

varieties.name: Trafalgar F1
varieties.text: A later sprout with firm buttons for winter picking. A useful partner to an earlier-cropping variety.

varieties.name: Brigitte F1
varieties.text: A modern Brussels sprout producing firm, well-shaped buttons. A strong candidate for the main autumn and winter crop.

varieties.name: Maximus F1
varieties.text: An early-to-mid-season hybrid. Useful for starting the sprout harvest before later winter selections are ready.

varieties.name: Crispus F1
varieties.text: A hybrid with clubroot resistance for affected plots. Continue using rotation and good growing conditions; resistance is not immunity.

reserves.name: PEER GYNT
reserves.text: An early, compact F1 hybrid with medium-sized buttons. Useful for autumn picking.
reserves.short_text: An early, compact F1 hybrid with medium-sized buttons. Useful for autumn picking.

reserves.name: OLIVER
reserves.text: An early variety for picking in September or October - the plants are quite short but the sprouts are large. The flavour is good and the yields are high.
reserves.short_text: An early variety for picking in September or October - the plants are quite short but the sprouts are large. The flavour is good and the yields are high.

reserves.name: CITADEL
reserves.text: A late F1 hybrid with round, dark green sprouts. Useful for winter picking.
reserves.short_text: A late F1 hybrid with round, dark green sprouts. Useful for winter picking.

reserves.name: WIDGEON
reserves.text: A winter-cropping hybrid. Choose healthy stock and pick firm buttons regularly.
reserves.short_text: A winter-cropping hybrid. Choose healthy stock and pick firm buttons regularly.

reserves.name: DOLMIC
reserves.text: An early F1 hybrid with tall plants and dark green, round-oval sprouts. Give it fertile soil and steady moisture.
reserves.short_text: An early F1 hybrid with tall plants and dark green, round-oval sprouts. Give it fertile soil and steady moisture.

reserves.name: SHERIFF
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid for late picking. Harvest small, firm buttons regularly through its season.
reserves.short_text: An F1 hybrid for late picking. Harvest small, firm buttons regularly through its season.

reserves.name: RAMPART
reserves.text: Another late variety which holds its sprouts for a long period without blowing. Tall-growing - the sprouts are quite large and noted for their flavour.
reserves.short_text: Another late variety which holds its sprouts for a long period without blowing. Tall-growing - the sprouts are quite large and noted for their flavour.

reserves.name: FORTRESS
reserves.text: A very late F1 hybrid on tall plants. It produces round, dark green sprouts.
reserves.short_text: A very late F1 hybrid on tall plants. It produces round, dark green sprouts.

reserves.name: TROIKA
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid for winter picking. Harvest firm buttons as they mature.
reserves.short_text: An F1 hybrid for winter picking. Harvest firm buttons as they mature.

reserves.name: EARLY HALF TALL
reserves.text: An alternative choice to the F1 hybrid Peer Gynt if you want a compact plant which will crop between September and Christmas.
reserves.short_text: An alternative choice to the F1 hybrid Peer Gynt if you want a compact plant which will crop between September and Christmas.

reserves.name: BEDFORD
reserves.text: The market gardeners of Bedfordshire originated this variety, noted for its large sprouts on tall stems. There are Bedford-Fillbasket if you want the heaviest yields and the largest sprouts, and Bedford-Asmer Monitor if you want a compact plant for a small garden.
reserves.short_text: The market gardeners of Bedfordshire originated this variety, noted for its large sprouts on tall stems. There are Bedford-Fillbasket if you want the heaviest yields and the largest sprouts, and Bedford-Asmer Monitor if you want a compact plant for a small garden.

reserves.name: NOISETTE
reserves.text: An old variety with small buttons and a pronounced nutty flavour. Sow in April or May, plant from May to early July, and harvest from October to March.
reserves.short_text: An old variety with small buttons and a pronounced nutty flavour. Sow in April or May, plant from May to early July, and harvest from October to March.

reserves.name: RUBINE
reserves.text: A red sprout with stronger colour after frost. It can be served raw in salads or cooked like green sprouts; harvest from October to March.
reserves.short_text: A red sprout with stronger colour after frost. It can be served raw in salads or cooked like green sprouts; harvest from October to March.

reserves.name: CAMBRIDGE NO. 5
reserves.text: An older, late variety producing large sprouts. Check availability with specialist suppliers.
reserves.short_text: An older, late variety producing large sprouts. Check availability with specialist suppliers.

reserves.name: ROODNERF
reserves.text: A group of varieties - Roodnerf-Seven Hills, Roodnerf-Early Button, etc., which keep their sprouts without blowing for a longer period than other standard sprouts.
reserves.short_text: A group of varieties - Roodnerf-Seven Hills, Roodnerf-Early Button, etc., which keep their sprouts without blowing for a longer period than other standard sprouts.

varieties.name: Greyhound
varieties.text: Traditional pointed summer cabbage; open-pollinated.

varieties.name: Hispi
varieties.text: Fast pointed heads for tender summer crops in small spaces.

varieties.name: Duncan F1
varieties.text: A versatile pointed cabbage for spring greens or hearted heads.

varieties.name: Tundra
varieties.text: Hardy, firm-headed winter cabbage for fresh supplies in colder months.

varieties.name: Red Drumhead
varieties.text: Traditional red heads for slaws, cooking and pickling.

varieties.name: Vertus
varieties.text: A late savoy with dense heads and crinkled leaves for winter harvests.

reserves.name: APRIL
reserves.text: Highly recommended - very early, compact and reliable. The shape is conical and there are few outer leaves.

reserves.name: SPRING HERO
reserves.text: An F1 spring cabbage with round heads weighing up to about 2 lb. Sow in late summer for the following spring.

reserves.name: PRIMO (GOLDEN ACRE)
reserves.text: The favourite ball-headed summer cabbage - compact and very firm.

reserves.name: STONEHEAD
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid which produces heavy round heads, although the plants are compact enough to allow close planting in beds. Stands well without splitting.

reserves.name: JANUARY KING
reserves.text: Drum-headed savoy type of cabbage - you can tell it by its red-tinged leaves. A December-January variety.

reserves.name: HOLLAND LATE WINTER
reserves.text: The old favourite white cabbage for coleslaw and storage.

reserves.name: WIROSA
reserves.text: A good choice if you want to gather good quality heads on Christmas Day.

reserves.name: DURHAM EARLY
reserves.text: Dark green and conical. Popular, especially as a source of spring greens. An early-maturing type producing medium-sized heads.

reserves.name: MYATT'S OFFENHAM COMPACTA (OFFENHAM 1)
reserves.text: A broad-leaved, dark green variety for sowing in early August and cutting in May. Grow for greens and heads.

reserves.name: FIRST EARLY MARKET 218
reserves.text: The one to choose if you want a large-headed spring cabbage. The heads are conical and dark green.

reserves.name: PIXIE
reserves.text: Small and tightly packed heads make this early variety an ideal choice for close planting in beds. A replacement for the old variety Dwarf March.

reserves.name: FLOWER OF SPRING (OFFENHAM 2)
reserves.text: No worries about the weather with this one - it is very hardy. The conical heads are large and solid.

reserves.name: DERBY DAY
reserves.text: Small round heads from a late winter greenhouse sowing or early spring start; useful for a June crop.

reserves.name: MINICOLE
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid which is becoming increasingly popular. The small, oval heads are produced in early autumn and will stand for up to 3 months without splitting.

reserves.name: WINNIGSTADT
reserves.text: An old favourite - the large, pointed heads are ready for cutting in September or October.

reserves.name: CELTIC
reserves.text: The crown prince of winter cabbages - an F1 hybrid of a savoy and winter white cabbage. Ball-headed, rock-hard, blue-green and capable of standing for months without splitting.

reserves.name: CHRISTMAS DRUMHEAD
reserves.text: The early one - dwarf, blue-green and ready from late October.

reserves.name: FILDERKRAUT
reserves.text: An old German white cabbage with sweet, pointed hearts in late autumn. Dense heads store well if cut before hard frost.

reserves.name: MARNER LAGERROT
reserves.text: A red storage cabbage. Cut dense hearts in November and store for winter use.

reserves.name: BEST OF ALL
reserves.text: The standard choice if you want a large drum-headed type which will mature in September.

reserves.name: ORMSKIRK LATE
reserves.text: The other end of the scale - this old favourite does not reach cutting size until February or March. The heads are large and dark green.

reserves.name: SAVOY KING
reserves.text: This F1 hybrid has been hailed by many as the best savoy of all. The foliage is light green - unusual for a savoy - and the heads are unsurpassed for size. Sow early for a September crop.

reserves.name: ORMSKIRK
reserves.text: A very hardy savoy with dark, heavily crinkled leaves. Valuable for winter and early spring use, sometimes cutting as late as March or April.

reserves.name: RUBY BALL
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid from America - claimed to be an improvement on earlier varieties. There are few outer leaves and the round heart is firm. Ready for cutting in late summer.

reserves.name: HARDORA
reserves.text: A late-maturing cabbage for storing, but you will have to hunt for a supplier.

reserves.name: TIP TOP
reserves.text: A Chinese cabbage with large heads, up to about 2 lb. Sow in summer and keep growth steady.

reserves.name: KASUMI
reserves.text: A reliable barrel type with good bolt resistance, but the heads are not tightly packed.

reserves.name: PE-TSAI (TYPE)
reserves.text: A general name for heading Chinese cabbage, rather than one distinct cultivar. Choose a named selection suited to the intended sowing season.

reserves.name: JADE PAGODA
reserves.text: A Michihili type - the heads are taller and thinner than the others described here.

varieties.name: Redskin
varieties.text: Compact sweet pepper for pots or small greenhouses; green fruit ripens red.

varieties.name: California Wonder
varieties.text: Familiar blocky sweet pepper. Pick green or ripen red in warm protection.

varieties.name: Corno di Toro Rosso
varieties.text: Long, tapering, thin-skinned red sweet peppers for cooking; an alternative to bells.

varieties.name: Demon Red
varieties.text: Compact chilli for pots, with small, hot fruit. Give warmth and shelter.

varieties.name: Habanero Orange
varieties.text: Very hot orange chilli needing a long, warm growing season.

varieties.name: Redskin
varieties.text: Compact sweet pepper for pots or small greenhouses; green fruit ripens red.

varieties.name: California Wonder
varieties.text: Familiar blocky sweet pepper. Pick green or ripen red in warm protection.

varieties.name: Corno di Toro Rosso
varieties.text: Long, tapering, thin-skinned red sweet peppers for cooking; an alternative to bells.

varieties.name: Demon Red
varieties.text: Compact chilli for pots, with small, hot fruit. Give warmth and shelter.

varieties.name: Habanero Orange
varieties.text: Very hot orange chilli needing a long, warm growing season.

reserves.name: NEW ACE
reserves.text: A good all-purpose pepper - early, high yielding and more tolerant of cool conditions than most varieties.

reserves.name: GYPSY
reserves.text: An early F1 sweet pepper with pale green fruits that ripen red. Give it warmth, regular watering and support when laden.

reserves.name: MARCONI ROSSA
reserves.text: A long sweet pepper, pale green at first and ripening red. Sow in February or March; grow about 30 in. high and stake or tie loosely. First harvest is normally July or August under cover.

reserves.name: ORANGE BABY
reserves.text: A smaller, sweet-fruited pepper on a compact plant. Useful for a large patio pot; sow in February or March and harvest from July or August under cover.

reserves.name: HUNGARIAN HOT WAX
reserves.text: A hot wax chilli, picked pale yellow or left to ripen red. Heat varies with strain, growing conditions and ripeness; do not assume immature fruit is mild. Sow in February or March and grow under cover for reliable UK crops.

reserves.name: HABANERO
reserves.text: A small orange chilli with extreme heat. Sow in February or March and treat as a greenhouse crop. First harvest is normally July or August - eater beware.

varieties.name: Early Nantes 2
varieties.text: A familiar early carrot with cylindrical roots. A practical general-purpose choice for successive sowings and tender young carrots.

varieties.name: Autumn King
varieties.text: A maincrop carrot producing substantial roots for autumn lifting and storage. Suits gardeners wanting a later, heavier crop.

varieties.name: Chantenay Red Cored
varieties.text: A shorter, broad-shouldered carrot. A useful alternative where very long-rooted varieties are less convenient to grow.

varieties.name: Early Nantes 2
varieties.text: A familiar early carrot with cylindrical roots. A practical general-purpose choice for successive sowings and tender young carrots.

varieties.name: Autumn King
varieties.text: A maincrop carrot producing substantial roots for autumn lifting and storage. Suits gardeners wanting a later, heavier crop.

varieties.name: Chantenay Red Cored
varieties.text: A shorter, broad-shouldered carrot. A useful alternative where very long-rooted varieties are less convenient to grow.

reserves.name: AMSTERDAM FORCING
reserves.text: Reputed to be the earliest of all for growing in the open or under cloches - cylindrical with a blunt stump end. There is little core and it is an excellent carrot for freezing.
reserves.short_text: Earliest cylindrical type; little core, good under cloches and for freezing.

reserves.name: JAMES SCARLET INTERMEDIATE
reserves.text: An old favourite with a good reputation for all-round performance. It is half-long, broad and tapered.
reserves.short_text: Reliable all-rounder; half-long, broad and tapered.

reserves.name: FLAKKEE
reserves.text: Like Autumn King, this Dutch variety has roots which are too long to warrant the label intermediate. But they are blunt-ended and so cannot be classed with the long-rooted varieties.

reserves.name: EARLY FRENCH FRAME
reserves.text: A round carrot - an excellent choice for shallow soils. It can reach 2 in. across but is best harvested before reaching such a mature stage. The variety Rondo belongs to this group.

reserves.name: EARLY SCARLET HORN
reserves.text: A good carrot of the Nantes type which is recommended for sowing under cloches in early March.

reserves.name: SYSTAN
reserves.text: This Nantes-type carrot is claimed to have some carrot fly resistance - the intermediate-rooted Fly Away claims even more.

reserves.name: KUNDULUS
reserves.text: A good carrot for bad soils, say the catalogues. The short cylindrical roots are almost ball-like - a wise choice for the small plot.

reserves.name: BERLICUM BERJO
reserves.text: An improvement on the old variety Berlicum - the cylindrical roots are stump-ended and it has a good reputation for keeping well, high yields and attractive colour.
reserves.short_text: Cylindrical, stump-ended; good keeper with high yields.

reserves.name: MOKUM
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid which produces cylindrical roots up to 9 in. long. It matures very rapidly, and can be sown from March until July.
reserves.short_text: F1 hybrid; fast-maturing cylindrical roots, sow Mar–Jul.

reserves.name: NANTES TIP TOP
reserves.text: The aristocrat of the Nantes group - a popular choice for showing. The 6 in. roots are uniformly cylindrical and core-free.

reserves.name: RAINBOW MIX
reserves.text: A colourful mixed selection rather than a single traditional variety. It is grown for its range of colours, flavours and vigour, and is useful for gardeners who want something more varied than the usual orange roots.

reserves.name: NEW RED INTERMEDIATE
reserves.text: Despite its name, one of the longest of all carrots. It has good keeping qualities.

reserves.name: ST VALERY
reserves.text: This is the one which the exhibitors so often choose. The roots are long, uniform and finely tapered.
reserves.short_text: Exhibitors' choice; long, uniform and finely tapered roots.

varieties.name: Clapton F1
varieties.text: A clubroot-resistant white cauliflower; combine with good rotation and soil care.

varieties.name: All The Year Round
varieties.text: White heads for successive sowings; not an all-year outdoor crop.

varieties.name: Graffiti
varieties.text: Purple heads add colour alongside white varieties.

varieties.name: Veronica F1
varieties.text: Pointed lime-green Romanesco curds offer distinctive shape and texture.

varieties.name: Aalsmeer
varieties.text: An overwintering type for spring crops. Sow in early summer; protect through winter.

varieties.text: Pointed lime-green Romanesco curds offer distinctive shape and texture.

varieties.name: Aalsmeer
varieties.text: An overwintering type for spring crops. Sow in early summer; protect through winter.

reserves.name: SNOWBALL
reserves.text: An early white cauliflower with fairly small, tight heads. Snow Crown is a distinct F1 hybrid of the Snowball type, producing heads around 2 lb.

reserves.name: ALPHA
reserves.text: An early cauliflower type with several selections. Follow the named selection’s sowing window; do not assume different Alpha selections have identical maturity or resistance to growth checks.

reserves.name: IGLOO
reserves.text: A summer cauliflower suited to mini heads. Space about 6 in. each way for small heads and harvest promptly.

reserves.name: AUTUMN GIANT
reserves.text: An established type with several selections, grown for large heads in early winter - Veitch's Self Protecting is the usual selection but there are others.

reserves.name: DOK-ELGON
reserves.text: An established cauliflower for late-summer cutting. Its performance depends on season and growing conditions; keep plants growing steadily.

reserves.name: BAMBI
reserves.text: A mini-cauliflower for small heads. Sow directly or transplant carefully, spacing about 6 in. each way and cutting promptly.

reserves.name: DOMINANT
reserves.text: A mid-season variety which matures in July. Good for freezing - its heads are large and its constitution is robust.

reserves.name: SNOWCAP
reserves.text: A white cauliflower retained from the legacy list. The name has been used for different selections; follow the seed supplier’s sowing and harvest dates rather than assuming winter hardiness.

reserves.name: FLORA BLANCA
reserves.text: Another name for the old favourite Autumn Glory. Grow this one for the autumn show - giant, pure white heads are ready for cutting in September and October.

reserves.name: CANBERRA
reserves.text: A popular Australian variety which matures in November. The curds are well protected by the broad leaves.

reserves.name: BARRIER REEF
reserves.text: Another Australian variety with the usual characteristics - compact growth and good curd cover by the leaves. It is ready for cutting from late October onwards.

reserves.name: ENGLISH WINTER
reserves.text: This was once the basic hardy variety, producing large heads between March and June. The numerous strains include St George (April), Leamington (April) and Late June (June).

reserves.name: WALCHEREN WINTER
reserves.text: An established Dutch overwintering cauliflower type with several selections. Armado April, Markanta and Maystar are retained as distinct named selections with their own spring harvest windows; check the supplier’s dates.

reserves.name: ST AGNES
reserves.text: A typical Roscoff variety, maturing as early as December. Sounds attractive - cauliflower for Christmas Dinner, but all the Roscoffs are frost-sensitive. Suitable only for the south west.

reserves.name: VILNA
reserves.text: An overwintering cauliflower for late-spring cutting. Protect developing curds from severe weather and harvest before the heads loosen.

reserves.name: PURPLE CAPE
reserves.text: A hardy overwintering cauliflower producing purple heads in spring. It needs no blanching, the young leaves can also be cooked, and the curd turns green when cooked.

reserves.name: ROMANESCO
reserves.text: An Italian broccoli-cauliflower type with pointed pale green minarets in a dome-shaped head. It is attractive and finely flavoured, but caterpillars are fond of it too.

varieties.name: Prinz
varieties.text: A dependable celeriac for rounded roots and useful kitchen quality. A strong first choice for the main crop.

varieties.name: Monarch
varieties.text: A modern celeriac with pale flesh and comparatively smooth roots. A useful addition for easier preparation in the kitchen.

varieties.name: Asterix F1
varieties.text: An early hybrid producing large, round roots for autumn harvesting and storage. Useful bolting resistance helps support a dependable crop.

varieties.name: Giant Prague
varieties.text: A long-established celeriac with large roots. Retain as a heritage alternative where seed cost and traditional varieties matter.

reserves.name: Marble Ball
reserves.text: A well-known variety - medium-sized, globular and strongly flavoured. Stores well over winter.

reserves.name: Iram
reserves.text: Medium-sized like Marble Ball, but remains white when cooked.

reserves.name: Tellus
reserves.text: Another variety which remains white after boiling. Quick-growing with a smoother skin than most varieties.

reserves.name: Balder
reserves.text: Medium-sized roots with a strong celery flavour. Keep growth steady through the full season.

reserves.name: Snow White
reserves.text: A nutty flavour, according to the suppliers. Large and white when cooked.

varieties.name: Victoria F1
varieties.text: Self-blanching celery with crisp, pale stalks. Easier than trench types.

varieties.name: Golden Self-Blanching
varieties.text: Traditional pale self-blanching celery. Water regularly for tender stalks.

varieties.name: Green Utah
varieties.text: Green-stemmed celery with a strong flavour. Keep moist for steady growth and tender stalks.

varieties.name: Giant Red
varieties.text: Red-stemmed trench celery with a strong flavour. Needs blanching and winter protection.

varieties.name: Victoria F1
varieties.text: Self-blanching celery with crisp, pale stalks. Easier than trench types.

varieties.name: Golden Self-Blanching
varieties.text: Traditional pale self-blanching celery. Water regularly for tender stalks.

varieties.name: Green Utah
varieties.text: Green-stemmed celery with a strong flavour. Keep moist for steady growth and tender stalks.

varieties.name: Giant Red
varieties.text: Red-stemmed trench celery with a strong flavour. Needs blanching and winter protection.

reserves.name: Giant White
reserves.text: The traditional white-stalked celery, tall and crisp and full of flavour, but demands good growing conditions. Various strains are sold by seed suppliers - you may find Solid White, Hopkins Fenlander or Brydon Prize White in the catalogue. Prizetaker is a popular choice for the show bench.

reserves.name: Dwarf White
reserves.text: A short-growing variety which needs less careful blanching than Giant White.

reserves.name: Giant Pink
reserves.text: A hardy variety for use in January or February. The crisp stalks form a solid heart and the pale pink sticks blanch easily. It may be listed as Unrivalled Pink - the strain Clayworth Prize Pink has a good reputation.

reserves.name: White Pascal
reserves.text: A large pure white variety with firm hearts for cutting from late autumn to December, but you will have to search for a supplier.

reserves.name: Lathom Self-Blanching
reserves.text: An established self-blanching celery with a vigorous habit and relatively short, ribbed stems. Harvest promptly for good flavour and tenderness.

reserves.name: Celebrity
reserves.text: An established self-blanching variety with fairly short plants, ribbed stems and good flavour. Grow in blocks and keep evenly moist.

reserves.name: American Green
reserves.text: A traditional green celery type with pale green, crisp stems. Greensnap and Utah are named selections in the legacy list; do not assume every strain has identical maturity.

reserves.name: Celery Leaf
reserves.text: A leaf-celery type for repeated small pickings. Sow in spring or early summer, space about 10 in. each way and pick outer stems regularly.

varieties.name: Palla Rossa
varieties.text: A red, hearting radicchio with crisp leaves and a pleasantly bitter flavour. Useful for colourful salads and cooking.

varieties.name: Witloof
varieties.text: A forcing chicory grown for pale chicons. Lift mature roots and force them in darkness for a winter crop.

varieties.name: Variegata di Castelfranco
varieties.text: A variegated chicory for attractive salad leaves. Adds a different colour and form to the red radicchio selection.

varieties.name: Sugar Loaf
varieties.text: An upright, green hearting chicory for autumn salads. Specify the actual supplier's selection when choosing seed.

reserves.name: Normato

reserves.name: Crystal Head
reserves.text: A non-forcing chicory for leafy heads. Snowflake and Winter Fare are other selections; choose sowing and winter protection to suit the named selection.

varieties.name: Defender F1
varieties.text: A productive green courgette with useful virus resistance for repeat summer picking.

varieties.name: Early Gem F1
varieties.text: An early green courgette. Pick young and often for continued summer crops.

varieties.name: Parador F1
varieties.text: Easy-to-spot yellow fruits add colour alongside green varieties.

varieties.name: Astia F1
varieties.text: Compact plants for containers or small beds; pick young and often.

varieties.name: Tiger Cross F1
varieties.text: A dark-green, pale-striped marrow. Grow larger for stuffing while maintaining regular harvests.

varieties.name: Parador F1
varieties.text: Easy-to-spot yellow fruits add colour alongside green varieties.

varieties.name: Astia F1
varieties.text: Compact plants for containers or small beds; pick young and often.

varieties.name: Tiger Cross F1
varieties.text: A dark-green, pale-striped marrow. Grow larger for stuffing while maintaining regular harvests.

reserves.name: Zucchini
reserves.text: The classic dark green courgette, producing freely for salads or cooked dishes.

reserves.name: Green Bush
reserves.text: A traditional bush marrow name with several numbered strains. Check the packet for the specific selection and harvest size.

reserves.name: Rondo di Nizza
reserves.text: Round green courgettes; productive and good for stuffing when picked young.

reserves.name: Golden Zucchini
reserves.text: Older yellow courgette variety with creamy flesh and good flavour.

reserves.name: Gold Rush
reserves.text: A yellow-fruited courgette. Pick young fruits regularly for tender texture.

reserves.name: Soleil F1
reserves.text: A separate yellow-fruited courgette with a compact habit.

reserves.name: Supremo
reserves.text: A dark green courgette for regular young-fruit harvesting.

reserves.name: Diamant F1
reserves.text: A green-fruited hybrid, sometimes translated as Diamond in seed listings.

reserves.name: Onyx F1
reserves.text: A dark, glossy green hybrid courgette with long, cylindrical fruit.

reserves.name: All Green Bush
reserves.text: A compact, productive dark green courgette. Pick regularly while young.

reserves.name: Long Green Trailing
reserves.text: Large cylindrical marrow with pale stripes; suitable where size or show bench impact matters.

reserves.name: Long White Trailing
reserves.text: Large pale marrow with good storage qualities.

varieties.name: Passandra F1
varieties.text: An all-female mini cucumber with short, convenient fruits. Useful where smaller portions suit the household.

varieties.name: Carmen F1
varieties.text: An all-female greenhouse cucumber producing long, smooth fruits. A strong choice for a reliable protected summer crop.

varieties.name: Mini Munch F1
varieties.text: A greenhouse cucumber with small snack-sized fruits. Pick regularly to encourage a steady supply of young cucumbers.

varieties.name: Telegraph Improved
varieties.text: A traditional long greenhouse cucumber. Follow variety-specific flower-management advice rather than treating it as an all-female hybrid.

varieties.name: Passandra F1

varieties.name: Carmen F1
varieties.text: An all-female greenhouse cucumber producing long, smooth fruits. A strong choice for a reliable protected summer crop.

varieties.name: Mini Munch F1
varieties.text: A greenhouse cucumber with small snack-sized fruits. Pick regularly to encourage a steady supply of young cucumbers.

varieties.name: Telegraph Improved
varieties.text: A traditional long greenhouse cucumber. Follow variety-specific flower-management advice rather than treating it as an all-female hybrid.

reserves.name: Telegraph
reserves.text: An old variety, named when the telegraph was a new invention. Despite its age, Telegraph is still popular.

reserves.name: Pepinex
reserves.text: An all-female greenhouse cucumber with long fruits. Keep plants warm and evenly watered; remove any male flowers according to the packet.

reserves.name: Femspot
reserves.text: An all-female greenhouse cucumber with fruits about 10–12 in. long. It needs warm growing conditions and can set fruit without pollination.

reserves.name: La Diva
reserves.text: An open-pollinated, mainly female cucumber with small, smooth fruits for protected or warm outdoor growing. It can set fruit without pollination; follow the seed supplier’s flower guidance.

reserves.name: Butcher's Disease Resisting
reserves.text: An established greenhouse cucumber with long fruits and a less smooth skin than Telegraph. Its name is not a guarantee of resistance to every disease.

reserves.name: Conqueror
reserves.text: A traditional cucumber for an unheated greenhouse or frame once conditions are warm. The fruits are long and smooth; plants remain frost-tender.

reserves.name: Topsy
reserves.text: A traditional greenhouse selection. Follow the seed supplier’s sowing and growing instructions.

reserves.name: Petita
reserves.text: An all-female greenhouse cucumber with fruits about 8 in. long. Occasional male flowers may appear; remove them as directed by the supplier.

reserves.name: Birgit
reserves.text: An established greenhouse cucumber grown for long fruits. Keep warm and train on supports.

reserves.name: Euphya
reserves.text: An all-female F1 greenhouse cucumber with long fruits. The breeder lists intermediate resistance to powdery mildew; Tyria is a separate selection.

reserves.name: Rocky F1
reserves.text: A baby cucumber for greenhouse culture. Sow in spring and grow vertically; the small fruits are useful where large cucumbers would be wasted.

varieties.name: Marketmore 76
varieties.text: A well-established ridge cucumber for outdoor growing in a warm, sheltered position. Produces dark-green slicing fruits.

varieties.name: Bush Champion
varieties.text: A compact outdoor cucumber suited to smaller gardens and large containers. A useful alternative to vigorous trailing selections.

varieties.name: Burpless Tasty Green
varieties.text: A long-fruited outdoor cucumber for a sheltered summer bed. Provide support where practical and pick fruits regularly.

varieties.name: Crystal Lemon
varieties.text: An unusual cucumber with round, pale-yellow fruits. Pick young for the best texture; a novelty alongside a standard slicing variety.

varieties.name: Marketmore 76
varieties.text: A well-established ridge cucumber for outdoor growing in a warm, sheltered position. Produces dark-green slicing fruits.

varieties.name: Bush Champion
varieties.text: A compact outdoor cucumber suited to smaller gardens and large containers. A useful alternative to vigorous trailing selections.

varieties.name: Burpless Tasty Green
varieties.text: A long-fruited outdoor cucumber for a sheltered summer bed. Provide support where practical and pick fruits regularly.

varieties.name: Crystal Lemon
varieties.text: An unusual cucumber with round, pale-yellow fruits. Pick young for the best texture; a novelty alongside a standard slicing variety.

reserves.name: Marketmore
reserves.text: An outdoor cucumber with straight, dark green fruits about 8 in. long. Named Marketmore selections differ; check the seed packet for disease resistance.

reserves.name: La Diva
reserves.text: An open-pollinated, mainly female cucumber with small, smooth fruits for protected or warm outdoor growing. It can set fruit without pollination; follow the seed supplier’s flower guidance.

reserves.name: Burpee Hybrid
reserves.text: Vigorous and prolific - an excellent choice. The 9 in. cucumbers have a smooth, dark green skin and the plant is noted for its reliability.

reserves.name: Marion
reserves.text: An established F1 outdoor cucumber. Check the supplied strain for specific disease-resistance claims.

reserves.name: Long Green Ridge
reserves.text: A traditional long-fruited ridge cucumber. Grow in a sunny, sheltered position and allow pollinators access.

reserves.name: Bush Crop
reserves.text: A compact bush cucumber for small beds or containers. Allow pollinators access and pick regularly.

reserves.name: Paska
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid with glossy dark green fruit about 10 in. long. Resistant to powdery mildew.

reserves.name: Jazzer
reserves.text: The fruits are seedless and the plants have good disease resistance. The cucumbers are up to 9 in. long.

reserves.name: Yamato
reserves.text: Smooth-skinned thin fruits which grow about 1 ft long.

reserves.name: Kyoto
reserves.text: Produces long, straight and smooth cucumbers to rival the ones on the supermarket shelf.

reserves.name: Tokyo Slicer
reserves.text: A Japanese-style slicing cucumber with smooth, dark green fruit. Train on supports and pick regularly.

reserves.name: Venlo Pickling
reserves.text: An established gherkin for harvesting small. Bestal, Hokus and Conda are other selections; follow their own harvest guidance.

reserves.name: Crystal Apple
reserves.text: A round, pale cucumber grown for young salad fruits. Pick regularly before the seed cavity becomes coarse.

reserves.name: Passandra F1
reserves.text: Primarily a greenhouse or polytunnel favourite with excellent flavour and yield, but included here as a useful comparison when deciding between outdoor and protected cucumbers.

reserves.name: Rocky F1
reserves.text: A small-fruited or baby cucumber type. It can be grown under cover, but the small fruit are useful where frequent picking is possible.

varieties.name: Pancalieri
varieties.text: A curly endive with finely divided leaves and a pleasantly bitter flavour for mixed salads.

varieties.name: En Cornet de Bordeaux
varieties.text: A broad-leaved endive with a more upright habit. Gives the list a useful alternative to finely curled varieties.

varieties.name: Fine Maraichere
varieties.text: A fine, frizzy-leaved endive for adding texture and bitterness to mixed salads. Pick young leaves for a gentler flavour.

varieties.name: Pancalieri

varieties.name: En Cornet de Bordeaux
varieties.text: A broad-leaved endive with a more upright habit. Gives the list a useful alternative to finely curled varieties.

varieties.name: Fine Maraichere
varieties.text: A fine, frizzy-leaved endive for adding texture and bitterness to mixed salads. Pick young leaves for a gentler flavour.

reserves.name: Batavian Green
reserves.text: An established broad-leaved endive. The official catalogue links Batavian Green and No 5 2 to Nummer Vijf 2.

reserves.name: Eminence
reserves.text: A broad-leaved endive with a yellow heart. Check the supplied seed for its sowing season.

reserves.name: Bubikopf
reserves.text: A reliable broad-leaved variety with plentiful, smaller leaves and good self-blanching qualities.

reserves.name: Green Curled
reserves.text: A traditional green, curly-leaved endive. Moss Curled is also a recorded endive name; do not assume every supplier uses these labels for an identical selection.

reserves.name: Sally
reserves.text: Noted for its tight hearts of curly leaves. An easy variety with the advantage of being self-blanching in the centre.

varieties.name: Zefa Fino
varieties.text: An established Florence fennel grown for swollen leaf bases. Keep growth steady with moisture and use appropriate sowing dates.

varieties.name: Romanesco
varieties.text: A traditional Florence fennel with substantial bulbs. Retain for gardeners who prefer a familiar non-hybrid selection.

varieties.name: Rondo F1
varieties.text: A modern Florence fennel producing rounded bulbs. A useful addition to the established open-pollinated choices.

varieties.name: Romanesco

varieties.name: Rondo F1
varieties.text: A modern Florence fennel producing rounded bulbs. A useful addition to the established open-pollinated choices.

reserves.name: Finale
reserves.text: An open-pollinated selection with large, flattened bulbs and useful bolting resistance

varieties.name: Solent Wight
varieties.text: A softneck garlic well suited to UK gardens and storage. A useful first choice for a dependable household crop.

varieties.name: Germidour
varieties.text: A softneck garlic with purple-marked skins. A familiar alternative for gardeners wanting large, useful bulbs.

varieties.name: Carcassonne Wight
varieties.text: A hardneck garlic providing an alternative to softneck types. It also produces edible flower stems, known as scapes.

varieties.name: Elephant
varieties.text: Produces very large, mild cloves. Grow as a separate culinary option; it is a leek relative rather than true garlic.

reserves.name: Spanish Roja
reserves.text: A strongly flavoured hardneck with thin skins; plant in October–February for July lifting and remove tender scapes once the bud forms.

varieties.name: Nero di Toscana
varieties.text: A dark, strap-leaved kale for repeated picking. Its textured leaves are especially useful in soups, stews and winter cooking.

varieties.name: Reflex F1
varieties.text: A green curly kale for productive winter picking. A useful maincrop choice where familiar curled leaves are preferred.

varieties.name: Red Russian
varieties.text: A flat-leaved kale with purple stems and tender young leaves. Useful for salads when young and cooking when larger.

varieties.name: Redbor F1
varieties.text: A purple-red curly kale that adds colour to the plot. Pick regularly for tender leaves and continued growth.

varieties.name: Yurok F1
varieties.text: A dark-leaved kale in the Tuscan style. Retain as a modern alternative where this leaf shape is preferred.

varieties.name: Red Russian

varieties.name: Redbor F1

varieties.name: Yurok F1
varieties.text: A dark-leaved kale in the Tuscan style. Retain as a modern alternative where this leaf shape is preferred.

reserves.name: Dwarf Green Curled
reserves.text: A compact curly kale for smaller plots, giving repeated pickings of green leaves. Stake if needed on an exposed site.

reserves.name: Cottagers
reserves.text: A heritage kale with green and purple foliage, grown for winter leaves and spring side shoots.

reserves.name: Tall Green Curled
reserves.text: The grown-up version of Dwarf Green Curled. Sometimes listed as Tall Scotch Curled. Suitable for freezing, as are all the curly-leaved varieties listed here.

reserves.name: Fribor
reserves.text: An F1 curly kale with dark green leaves. Check the seed packet for mature size and spacing.

reserves.name: Westland Autumn
reserves.text: A curly-leaved kale grown for autumn and winter greens. Check the seed packet for its mature size and picking season.

reserves.name: Spurt
reserves.text: A curly-leaved kale that can be sown directly or transplanted. Harvest young leaves while tender; maturity depends on sowing date and growing conditions.

reserves.name: Darkibor
reserves.text: A dark green F1 curly kale. Allow space for its mature spread and pick tender leaves regularly.

reserves.name: Thousand-headed Kale
reserves.text: A productive traditional kale, also known as Thousand Head, grown for leaves and tender spring shoots.

reserves.name: Hungry Gap
reserves.text: A late cropper, like all Rape kales. Robust and reliable, producing shoots which are suitable for freezing.

reserves.name: Asparagus Kale
reserves.text: Grown especially for tender spring shoots; young leaves can also be eaten.

reserves.name: Pentland Brig
reserves.text: A cross between a curly-leaved kale and a plain-leaved one. Plants grow about 2 ft tall, and their kitchen use differs from other kales. Pick young leaves from the crown beginning in November - they are fringed but less so than a curly-leaved kale. In early spring harvest the leafy side shoots and later gather the immature flower-heads, or spears, which should be cooked like broccoli.

reserves.name: Sutherland
reserves.text: A flat-leaved type noted for good flavour.

varieties.name: Kolibri F1
varieties.text: A quick-growing purple kohlrabi with crisp white flesh. Pick the swollen stems young for tender raw or cooked slices.

varieties.name: Kossak F1
varieties.text: A pale-green kohlrabi with mild white flesh. A useful modern alternative to the traditional Vienna selections.

varieties.name: White Superschmelz
varieties.text: A large-growing pale kohlrabi. Useful for gardeners wanting a substantial crop rather than very small, quick-picked stems.

varieties.name: Green Vienna
varieties.text: An early variety with green skin and white flesh. Sow in spring or summer.

varieties.name: Lanro
varieties.text: An open-pollinated variety with pale green globes and white flesh. Pick them young while they are tender.

varieties.name: Purple Vienna
varieties.text: A useful choice for a late crop. Pick the purple-skinned globes while they are still young and tender.

varieties.text: A quick-growing purple kohlrabi with crisp white flesh. Pick the swollen stems young for tender raw or cooked slices.

varieties.name: Kossak F1
varieties.text: A pale-green kohlrabi with mild white flesh. A useful modern alternative to the traditional Vienna selections.

varieties.name: White Superschmelz
varieties.text: A large-growing pale kohlrabi. Useful for gardeners wanting a substantial crop rather than very small, quick-picked stems.

varieties.name: Green Vienna
varieties.text: An early variety with green skin and white flesh. Sow in spring or summer.

varieties.name: Lanro
varieties.text: An open-pollinated variety with pale green globes and white flesh. Pick them young while they are tender.

varieties.name: Purple Vienna
varieties.text: A useful choice for a late crop. Pick the purple-skinned globes while they are still young and tender.

reserves.name: Rowel
reserves.text: A named kohl rabi selection. Keep moisture steady and harvest while tender; do not assume oversized globes will remain free of woodiness.

varieties.name: Musselburgh
varieties.text: A traditional hardy leek with thick stems for dependable autumn and winter crops.

varieties.name: Oarsman F1
varieties.text: A modern autumn leek with useful rust resistance and healthy foliage.

varieties.name: Jolant
varieties.text: An earlier crop for late summer and autumn, complementing hardy winter leeks.

varieties.name: Below Zero F1
varieties.text: A winter leek for standing through cold weather and extending fresh picking.

reserves.name: Porvite
reserves.text: An autumn to early winter leek which can give good, consistent results where a reliable main-season crop is wanted.

reserves.name: Lyon 2-Prizetaker
reserves.text: Also known as Prizetaker or Lyon. A traditional long-stemmed autumn leek for exhibition and the kitchen; harvest before severe winter weather.

reserves.name: Splendid
reserves.text: A Gennevilliers strain for autumn harvesting, with white shanks around 6 in. long.

reserves.name: Walton Mammoth
reserves.text: A traditional large autumn leek, used for exhibition and the kitchen. Follow the supplier’s harvest window rather than relying on it for severe-winter cropping.

reserves.name: King Richard
reserves.text: An early leek with pale green leaves and long white shanks, potentially around 12 in. with careful blanching.

reserves.name: Swiss Giant
reserves.text: One of the earliest and longest-stemmed leeks, suitable for harvest from August to November. It grows fast and gives long white shanks, but dislikes hard frost and should be lifted before severe winter weather.

reserves.name: Autumn Mammoth
reserves.text: A reliable autumn leek, best before Christmas. Similar strains include Tornado and Goliath; all are useful for heavy autumn crops but should not be relied on as the latest winter leeks.

reserves.name: Snowstar
reserves.text: A winter leek with short, thick stems and dark foliage, similar in appearance to Musselburgh.

reserves.name: Argenta
reserves.text: A mid-season leek with a mild flavour and white shanks around 5 in. long, for late-autumn and winter harvesting.

reserves.name: Goliath
reserves.text: A large autumn leek in the Autumn Mammoth group. Retain as a separate named selection from Argenta and follow its supplier’s harvest dates.

reserves.name: Giant Winter-Catalina
reserves.text: A Giant Winter selection producing thick stems for winter harvesting. Check the supplier’s harvest window for the particular strain.

reserves.name: Winterreuzen
reserves.text: A Giant Winter type with several named or numbered selections. Follow the strain’s harvest window; do not assume every Winterreuzen selection is identical.

reserves.name: Yates Empire
reserves.text: Looks like Musselburgh with thick, pure white stems but it will stand in the ground quite happily until mid April.

reserves.name: Winter Crop
reserves.text: A hardy winter leek useful for exposed sites; local conditions still affect how long plants remain in good condition.

reserves.name: Bandit
reserves.text: A hardy, long, late-to-flower leek for February to April harvests. Useful where a crop is wanted to stand well into spring.

reserves.name: Apollo
reserves.text: A spring leek that can continue into early May and grows rapidly through April, giving useful harvests when few other vegetables are available.

reserves.name: St Victor
reserves.text: A spring variety with attractive violet-coloured leaves. It is useful in the bleakest part of the year and carries on into spring, but should be harvested before flower buds harden the stems.

varieties.name: Little Gem
varieties.text: Compact, crisp, sweet cos hearts for small gardens and repeat sowings.

varieties.name: Salad Bowl
varieties.text: Loose leaves for small, repeated pickings without harvesting a whole head.

varieties.name: Winter Density
varieties.text: Compact, cooler-season lettuce; use protection to extend salad harvests.

varieties.name: All The Year Round
varieties.text: Familiar butterhead for successive sowings; a soft-leaved alternative to cos and loose-leaf.

varieties.name: Lollo Rossa
varieties.text: Frilled red loose-leaf for colour and texture. Pick outer leaves or take whole young plants.

reserves.name: Lobjoits Green
reserves.text: Large green cos with crisp, self-folding leaves and a well-blanched heart. Keep growth steady; tipburn can occur.

reserves.name: Tom Thumb
reserves.text: The favourite for small plots, producing heads which are tennis ball size. Quick-maturing, fine-flavoured and grown at a summer crop.

reserves.name: Buttercrunch
reserves.text: The central heart of creamy leaves is hard and compact - crunchy enough to make some books list it with the crispheads. An American variety.

reserves.name: Arctic King
reserves.text: Winter-hardy - the one to choose if you want a more compact spring lettuce than Imperial Winter.

reserves.name: Marvel of Four Seasons
reserves.text: Fine butterhead with waxy mottled bronze leaves; hardy enough for some late-summer sowings.

reserves.name: Webb's Wonderful
reserves.text: Large-hearted crisphead with frilly, crunchy leaves. Suitable for summer cropping; its leaves are more crinkled than true iceberg types.

reserves.name: Great Lakes
reserves.text: A large, spreading crisphead. It is the original summer crisphead lettuce which came to us from America.

reserves.name: Iceberg
reserves.text: You can buy the seed of this super-crisp white-hearted lettuce which has become so popular on supermarket shelves. Sow in spring or early summer.

reserves.name: Freckles
reserves.text: Green leaves spotted with dark red-brown. Productive but attractive to slugs.

reserves.name: Paris White
reserves.text: Like Lobjoits Green, this variety is popular, large, self-folding and crisp. The heart, however, is pale green.

reserves.name: Bubbles
reserves.text: A cos lettuce of the Little Gem type - useful where space is limited. Its unique feature is the highly crinkled or bubbled surface of the leaves.

reserves.name: Chartwell
reserves.text: Green cos lettuce suitable for repeated leaf picking or growing to a sweet heart.

reserves.name: Claremont
reserves.text: Green cos lettuce suitable for repeated leaf picking or growing to a sweet heart.

reserves.name: Rosemoor
reserves.text: Dark red, tender cos type with thinner leaves than green cos.

reserves.name: Avondefiance
reserves.text: Dark green butterhead for summer and autumn cropping, with resistance to lettuce root aphid. Keep plants growing steadily.

reserves.name: Continuity
reserves.text: The summer lettuce with the red-tinged leaves. Long-standing and compact - a good choice for sandy soils.

reserves.name: Dolly
reserves.text: Large butterhead for summer cropping. Keep growth steady and harvest hearts promptly.

reserves.name: Hilde
reserves.text: A popular choice for sowing under glass and planting out early to produce a May crop.

reserves.name: Suzan
reserves.text: Another variety which can be sown under glass in February or outdoors in spring to produce a summer crop. Hearts are large and pale green.

reserves.name: Winter Crop
reserves.text: One of the frost-hardy varieties suitable for sowing outdoors in August or September to produce a crop in spring.

reserves.name: Imperial Winter
reserves.text: Hardy butterhead for late-summer sowing and spring harvest. Also sold as Winter Marvel.

reserves.name: Kwiek
reserves.text: A popular forcing lettuce for growing under glass to produce an early winter crop.

reserves.name: Premier
reserves.text: A forcing variety for growing under glass. Sow in October for cropping in April. The pale green hearts are large.

reserves.name: May King
reserves.text: Early butterhead, also sold as May Queen. Sow under cover or cloches for an early crop; outer leaves can be red-tinged.

reserves.name: Kloek
reserves.text: A winter lettuce for cropping in January to March. A heated greenhouse is necessary - sow seed in September or October for large, solid hearts in midwinter when lettuce is scarce.

reserves.name: Musette
reserves.text: Dark green butterhead for summer and autumn, with reported resistance to root aphid, lettuce mosaic virus and downy mildew. Resistance is not immunity.

reserves.name: Windermere
reserves.text: Another excellent frilly crisphead for summer cropping - sow outdoors in March to July or under glass in February. Can be grown in a cold frame as a spring lettuce, preferred by some experts to Webb's Wonderful.

reserves.name: Avoncrisp
reserves.text: Frilly crisphead for summer or autumn use, with resistance to lettuce root aphid.

reserves.name: Lakeland
reserves.text: An Iceberg-type crisphead bred to be more reliable in Britain than the original Iceberg variety.

reserves.name: Marmres
reserves.text: Recommended for growing under glass. Iceberg-type. Sow in October in an unheated greenhouse and cut in April.

reserves.name: Bergamo
reserves.text: Vigorous, bright green Lollo Biondi type that crops steadily for a long period if picked regularly; slow to seed but first leaves are close to the soil.

reserves.name: Amorina
reserves.text: A larger, light cherry-coloured form of Bergamo. Attractive and long-cropping, though darker leaves tend to grow more slowly.

reserves.name: Belize
reserves.text: Oakleaf type with vibrant yellow-green leaves, capable of several months of picking.

reserves.name: Cocarde
reserves.text: A bronze version of Catalogna, vigorous and large-leaved; a little easier to pick than many oakleaf lettuces.

reserves.name: Maravilla de Verano
reserves.text: Batavian lettuce with substantial green leaves tinged with bronze-red. Useful for summer leaf picking or hearts.

reserves.name: Grenoble Red
reserves.text: Crisp green-and-bronze Batavian, also sold as Rouge Grenobloise. Useful for autumn and winter leaf picking under suitable protection.

reserves.name: Bijou
reserves.text: One of the darkest red cultivars; ornamental and useful for contrast in the garden and salad bowl.

varieties.name: Red Baron
varieties.text: Red bulbs for salads and cooking; available as seed or sets.

varieties.name: Sturon
varieties.text: A dependable brown storage onion, usually grown from sets.

varieties.name: Ailsa Craig
varieties.text: Large, mild bulbs from seed; useful in the kitchen rather than for long winter storage.

varieties.name: White Lisbon
varieties.text: A familiar salad onion with slender white stems; sow small batches for steady young pickings.

varieties.name: Jermor
varieties.text: A flavoursome, copper-skinned shallot with elongated bulbs, usually grown from sets.

varieties.name: Zebrune
varieties.text: A banana shallot from seed; elongated bulbs are easy to slice.

varieties.name: Red Baron
varieties.text: Red bulbs for salads and cooking; available as seed or sets.

varieties.name: Sturon
varieties.text: A dependable brown storage onion, usually grown from sets.

varieties.name: Ailsa Craig
varieties.text: Large, mild bulbs from seed; useful in the kitchen rather than for long winter storage.

varieties.name: White Lisbon
varieties.text: A familiar salad onion with slender white stems; sow small batches for steady young pickings.

varieties.name: Jermor
varieties.text: A flavoursome, copper-skinned shallot with elongated bulbs, usually grown from sets.

varieties.name: Zebrune
varieties.text: A banana shallot from seed; elongated bulbs are easy to slice.

reserves.name: Rijnsburger
reserves.text: Large, round, pale-skinned onions with white flesh. Several strains are sold, from seed or as sets; keeping quality depends on the strain and ripening.

reserves.name: North Holland Blood Red
reserves.text: Red-skinned bulbs useful for cooking, colour and exhibition; also usable young.

reserves.name: Santero
reserves.text: Mildew-resistant yellow onion; sow February-March; first harvest August.

reserves.name: Long Red Florence
reserves.text: Long bulbs with mild flavour; sow February-April; first harvest July.

reserves.name: Walla Walla
reserves.text: Very mild raw onion; can make a large bulb if given space.

reserves.name: Senshyu
reserves.text: A Japanese overwintering onion type. Check the named strain when buying; the short name alone does not establish that it is identical to Senshyu Semi-Globe Yellow.

reserves.name: Ishikura
reserves.text: Long, straight stems and no bulb; pull a few at a time.

reserves.name: Ramrod
reserves.text: A white salad onion with long stems; pull young. It may form a small bulb if left longer, so do not treat it as a guaranteed non-bulbing bunching onion.

reserves.name: White Lisbon Winter Hardy
reserves.text: Autumn-sown salad onion; sow August-early September; first harvest March.

reserves.name: Paris Silverskin
reserves.text: A small white onion for pickling or salad use. Sow in spring, grow close and lift small.

reserves.name: Bedfordshire Champion
reserves.text: Large, round bulbs suitable for storage. Keep foliage airy and watch for downy mildew.

reserves.name: Lancastrian
reserves.text: A traditional large, globe-shaped golden onion for exhibition and the kitchen.

reserves.name: Stuttgarter Giant
reserves.text: Also sold as Stuttgarter or Stuttgart Giant. Flat-round, yellow-brown bulbs with a mild flavour and good storage potential; commonly grown from spring-planted sets.

reserves.name: Turbo
reserves.text: A yellow storage onion commonly grown from spring-planted sets. Plant in March–April when soil conditions permit and harvest as foliage yellows.

reserves.name: Kelsae
reserves.text: Huge bulbs for maximum size if sown very early, often January; first harvest August.

reserves.name: Purplette
reserves.text: Small bulbs with many uses; sow February-May; first harvest June.

reserves.name: Buffalo
reserves.text: An F1 hybrid for an early bulb crop from suitable spring or late-summer sowings. Use early bulbs promptly; keeping depends on maturity and growing conditions.

reserves.name: Reliance
reserves.text: A traditional overwintering onion from late-summer seed, producing large, flattened bulbs. Dry thoroughly before storage.

reserves.name: Express Yellow
reserves.text: An early overwintering type with slightly flattened, yellow-skinned bulbs.

reserves.name: Kaizuka Extra Early
reserves.text: An early Japanese overwintering type with pale, slightly flattened bulbs.

reserves.name: Imai Yellow
reserves.text: A Japanese variety which is globe-shaped and early.

reserves.name: Radar
reserves.text: Overwintering onion from sets; plant September-October; first harvest June–July.

reserves.name: Senshyu Semi-Globe Yellow
reserves.text: Overwintering onion from seed; sow late August; first harvest June–July.

reserves.name: Electric
reserves.text: Autumn-planted red onion; plant September-October; first harvest June–July.

reserves.name: Barletta
reserves.text: Cocktail onion type for pickling.

reserves.name: Dutch Yellow
reserves.text: Older yellow shallot type, superseded in many lists by Golden Gourmet.

reserves.name: Hative de Niort
reserves.text: Exhibition shallot with well-shaped deep-brown bulbs.

reserves.name: Golden Gourmet
reserves.text: Round, golden shallot bulbs, usually planted as sets in spring for a midsummer harvest.

reserves.name: Red Sun
reserves.text: Round, reddish-brown shallot bulbs, usually planted as sets in spring for a midsummer harvest.

varieties.name: Mizuna
varieties.text: Quick Japanese leaf with finely cut foliage and mild mustard flavour for salads or brief cooking.

varieties.name: Mibuna
varieties.text: Narrow, strap-like Japanese green. Use young leaves in salads, larger ones in stir-fries.

varieties.name: Red Frills mustard
varieties.text: Finely divided, peppery red mustard. Pick young and mix with milder salad leaves.

varieties.name: Joi Choi
varieties.text: Crisp white-stalked pak choi with green leaves. Pick young for salads, larger for stir-fries.

varieties.name: Tatsoi
varieties.text: Low rosettes of dark leaves for baby-leaf salads and quick cooking.

reserves.name: Shungiku
reserves.text: Also called chop suey greens; chrysanthemum-family plant with a distinctive pungent flavour

reserves.name: Waido
reserves.text: A named mizuna selection with broader, less deeply cut leaves and white stems.

reserves.name: Chinese cabbage
reserves.text: Dense heart; pe-tsai type makes a heart and stores better than most leaves

reserves.name: Leaf radish
reserves.text: Large, mild leaves; a useful root crop depends on the variety.

reserves.name: Mustards
reserves.text: Hot, spicy leaves in red, green and golden forms, often long and serrated

reserves.name: Pak choi
reserves.text: Crunchy stems and mild, succulent leaves; green-stemmed forms make more smaller leaves for summer salads

varieties.name: Gladiator
varieties.text: A well-established hybrid parsnip producing useful, even roots. A strong first choice for the main autumn and winter crop.

varieties.name: Tender and True
varieties.text: A traditional parsnip with long roots and good flavour. Best grown in deep, stone-free soil.

varieties.name: Palace F1
varieties.text: An early-to-maincrop hybrid with smooth roots, shallow crowns and some canker resistance. A useful alternative to Gladiator.

varieties.name: White Gem
varieties.text: Sweet, stocky roots for shallower or heavier soil, with some canker resistance.

varieties.name: Hollow Crown Improved
varieties.text: Long, tapering roots for cooking or showing. Give them deep, loose soil without stones.

varieties.name: The Student
varieties.text: Medium-sized, thick, tapering roots with a sweet flavour.

reserves.name: Avonresister
reserves.text: Short, sweet-flavoured roots with canker resistance. Use the standard spacing in Sowing & Planting.

varieties.name: Kelvedon Wonder
varieties.text: Compact early shelling pea for small spaces and early harvests. Give short supports.

varieties.name: Hurst Green Shaft
varieties.text: Familiar maincrop shelling pea with long pods for generous pickings.

varieties.name: Oregon Sugar Pod
varieties.text: Whole, flat mangetout pods: pick before peas swell for tenderness.

varieties.name: Sugar Ann
varieties.text: Early sugar-snap pea with crisp, edible pods, contrasting with shelling and mangetout.

varieties.name: Alderman
varieties.text: Tall shelling pea; strong supports and extra height reward with longer picking.

varieties.name: Meteor
varieties.text: A compact round-seeded pea for colder or exposed sites. Useful for early crops.
