varieties.name: Meteor
varieties.text: A compact round-seeded pea for colder or exposed sites. Useful for early crops.

reserves.name: Douce Provence
reserves.text: Perhaps you are looking for maximum sweetness rather than maximum yield. Douce Provence is the one to choose - it has all the robustness of Feltham First but the flavour is superior. Height about 1 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Early Onward
reserves.text: More famous brother of the Second Early Onward; reliable. Height about 2 ft.

reserves.name: Onward
reserves.text: A reliable shelling pea with heavy crops of plump, blunt-ended, dark green pods. Give support; plants reach about 2 1/2 ft. March-April sowings may give a first harvest in about 90-95 days, depending on conditions.

reserves.name: Norli
reserves.text: Compact mangetout with sweet, flat pods, picked while the peas inside are tiny. Also sold as Sugar Dwarf Sweet Green. Give light support; sowing and cropping times depend on conditions.

reserves.name: Ambassador
reserves.text: Semi-leafless type; pods are easier to see and pick than on very leafy peas.

reserves.name: Feltham First
reserves.text: A compact round-seeded early pea, about 1 1/2 ft tall, with pointed pods about 4 in. long. Give light support. It is quick and hardy; cropping time depends on sowing date and conditions.

reserves.name: Pilot
reserves.text: Very popular as it combines earliness with a heavy crop. Best choice for a May to June crop. Height about 3 ft.

reserves.name: Fortune
reserves.text: Quite similar to Feltham First; matures rather later but yields may be higher. Height about 1 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Little Marvel
reserves.text: The flavour is good and the growth is robust. Height about 1 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Beagle
reserves.text: Sometimes listed as Hurst Beagle; the earliest wrinkled variety. Blunt-ended pods with 8 peas per pod. Height about 1 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Progress No. 9
reserves.text: Almost rivals Beagle in earliness; differs from it by bearing pointed pods. Height about 1 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Pioneer
reserves.text: A useful variety for early sowing and also for June sowing. It resists mildew. Height about 1 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Cavalier
reserves.text: Long pointed pods borne in pairs; yields are high and flavour is good. Mildew resistance makes it suitable for summer. Height about 2 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Bikini
reserves.text: One of the new less-leaf, more-tendril varieties. It is claimed that the tendrils can be boiled and eaten as a second vegetable. Other less-leaf peas are Ealon and Poppet. Height about 1 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Lord Chancellor
reserves.text: Late-maturing and claimed by some to be the best maincrop pea variety. Heavy cropper bearing dark green, pointed pods. Height about 3 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Gradus
reserves.text: This one is for sowing in April for a July crop. Pods are large and crops are heavy. Support is necessary. The flavour is rated very highly. Height about 3 ft.

reserves.name: Senator
reserves.text: Highly recommended as the maincrop for small gardens. The pods are borne in pairs; both flavour and yield are claimed to be exceptional. Height about 2 1/2 ft.

reserves.name: Gulliver
reserves.text: Once the basic type, now replaced in catalogues by Waverex. The pods and seeds are small, peas were delicious, but the plants were tall for such a tiny pea. Height about 3 ft.

reserves.name: Waverex
reserves.text: The petit pois you are most likely to find. Eat raw in salads or cook the French way. Height about 2 ft.

reserves.name: Cobri
reserves.text: An old variety which is still available. Typical petit pois for you to shell and cook. Boil in the pods and shell before serving, advises the main supplier. Height about 2 ft.

reserves.name: Sugar Snap
reserves.text: A dual-purpose pea. When pods are young they are cooked like mangetout. More mature pods with peas inside can be stringed and then cooked like french beans or shelled and cooked like peas. Height about 5 ft.

reserves.name: Edula
reserves.text: Like Sugar Snap, but more compact for the smaller garden. Height about 3 ft.

reserves.name: Tall Sugar Snap
reserves.text: Extra sweet edible snap-pods; tall plants can reach 5-6 1/2 ft or more and need strong sticks, posts or netting. First harvest about 85-90 days.

reserves.name: Sugar Bon
reserves.text: Compact sugar-snap pea with edible pods; support with short pea sticks or netting.

varieties.name: Charlotte
varieties.text: Second-early salad: firm yellow flesh for boiling or new potatoes.

varieties.name: Maris Piper
varieties.text: Floury maincrop potato for chips, roasting and mash.

varieties.name: Sarpo Mira
varieties.text: Vigorous red maincrop; strong blight resistance and floury mature flesh.

varieties.name: Casablanca
varieties.text: First-early for an early harvest; tender tubers when lifted young.

varieties.name: Desiree
varieties.text: Red-skinned maincrop with pale-yellow flesh for everyday cooking.

varieties.name: Pink Fir Apple
varieties.text: Late salad potato with knobbly tubers and firm, waxy flesh.

reserves.name: Arran Pilot
reserves.text: Long; white flesh. An old favourite, now being replaced by modern varieties. Heavy cropper with close-set eyes and softish skin in southern counties.

reserves.name: Duke of York
reserves.text: Oval, yellow-fleshed early potatoes with a traditional flavour; useful for boiling.

reserves.name: Rocket
reserves.text: Round; white flesh. A variety of the 1980s bred in Cambridge. It has become popular for the yields and egg-sized tubers. Tuber blight can be a problem.

reserves.name: Maris Bard
reserves.text: An early variety with oval, white-fleshed tubers, useful for fresh boiling. Check current supplier information for any specific disease-resistance claims.

reserves.name: Sharpe's Express
reserves.text: Long; white flesh. Once available everywhere, now pushed aside by newer varieties. Still a good choice for heavy soil. Rather late, but tubers store well.

reserves.name: Pentland Javelin
reserves.text: A first early with oval, white-fleshed tubers. Resistance to the golden potato cyst nematode does not imply resistance to every nematode species or population.

reserves.name: Nadine
reserves.text: Round; white flesh. One of the newer varieties steadily replacing old favourites. Smooth uniform tubers, good exhibition qualities and high flavour rating.

reserves.name: Wilja
reserves.text: Oval; pale yellow flesh. High yields, excellent cooking qualities and reliability account for its popularity.

reserves.name: Maris Peer
reserves.text: A second-early potato with oval, creamy-fleshed tubers useful for boiling and salads. Keep watered as tubers swell, particularly on light soil.

reserves.name: King Edward
reserves.text: Oval; creamy flesh. Red-blotched variety; one of the best known potatoes and still grown in many gardens where cooking quality rather than quantity is valued.

reserves.name: Cara
reserves.text: Round; creamy flesh. High-yielding potato that stores well; pink-eyed tubers are good for baking. Some blight resistance but drawbacks as a late maturing variety.

reserves.name: Ulster Sceptre
reserves.text: A traditional early potato with long, white-fleshed tubers. Retained as its own variety; Ulster Chieftain is a different name, not a synonym.

reserves.name: Epicure
reserves.text: A traditional round, white-fleshed early potato. It can recover after foliage frost damage, but protect emerging shoots: it is not frost-proof.

reserves.name: Vanessa
reserves.text: Long; yellow flesh. Red-skinned First Early, late to mature but succeeds better than most in dry weather.

reserves.name: Sutton's Foremost
reserves.text: An early potato also known as Foremost, with oval, white-fleshed tubers suitable for boiling. Use healthy seed and watch for pests and disease.

reserves.name: Sprint
reserves.text: An early potato. Follow the supplier’s maturity guidance, use normal early-potato spacing and test tuber size before lifting.

reserves.name: Stroma
reserves.text: Oval, pink-skinned tubers with yellowish flesh and a mild flavour.

reserves.name: Marfona
reserves.text: Round; creamy flesh. High yields of large round or short oval tubers. A good choice for sandy soil or for baking.

reserves.name: Estima
reserves.text: Oval, pale yellow-fleshed tubers with good cropping potential. A useful second early for general cooking; keep soil moist as tubers form to reduce scab.

reserves.name: Catriona
reserves.text: Long; creamy flesh. Popular with exhibitors because long yellow tubers with purple patches are eye-catching. Crops well but cannot be stored for long periods.

reserves.name: Majestic
reserves.text: Long; white flesh. Once recommended for nearly all uses, but now being pushed out. Still keeps its reputation as a fine potato for making chips.

reserves.name: Pentland Crown
reserves.text: A late maincrop with large, oval, white-fleshed tubers. Allow a long growing season.

reserves.name: Pentland Dell
reserves.text: Long; white flesh. High yields and good flavour but has problems. Suffers in cold soil in spring and tubers tend to blacken when cooked.

reserves.name: Golden Wonder
reserves.text: Long; yellow flesh. Best-flavoured potato according to many books, but generally needs well-manured soil and is susceptible to both drought and slugs. Tubers are small and yields low.

reserves.name: Kerr's Pink
reserves.text: Round; white flesh. Early Maincrop grown by people in wet and heavy soil areas who like a floury potato. Excellent chip potato.

reserves.name: Romano
reserves.text: A red-skinned, pale-fleshed maincrop useful for general cooking and storage. Keep growth steady with water during dry spells.

reserves.name: Remarka
reserves.text: A maincrop potato with yellow skin and yellow flesh. A general-purpose cooking type with medium dry matter, rather than a specifically waxy salad potato.

reserves.name: Stemster
reserves.text: A maincrop with pink-red skin and pale yellow flesh. Useful boiled, mashed, baked or roasted, with good storage potential and some suitability for drier soils.

varieties.name: French Breakfast 3
varieties.text: A familiar long red-and-white summer radish. Sow small batches; pick promptly for crisp, mildly peppery roots.

varieties.name: Cherry Belle
varieties.text: A round, bright-red salad radish for quick crops in beds or containers.

varieties.name: Scarlet Globe
varieties.text: A round red summer radish for quick, repeat crops. Harvest young before roots become coarse.

varieties.name: China Rose
varieties.text: A pink, long-rooted winter radish for autumn use, contrasting with round black storage types.

varieties.name: Black Spanish Round
varieties.text: A black-skinned winter radish with firm white flesh, grown for large autumn roots, not quick summer crops.

reserves.name: Sparkler
reserves.text: Round, red-and-white roots. Sow little and often; pull while young and crisp.

reserves.name: French Breakfast
reserves.text: Long red-and-white salad radish. Sow small batches from March to August; thin to the salad-radish spacing in Sowing & Planting. Pull while crisp and mild, before roots become hot and woody.

reserves.name: Long White Icicle
reserves.text: Long, white roots. Crisp, nutty-flavoured flesh; roots reach about 3 in. long.

reserves.name: Munchen Bier
reserves.text: Podding radish grown for edible pods as well as roots. Plants can reach about 2 ft tall; use pods raw or cooked.

reserves.name: Black Spanish Long
reserves.text: Long black winter radish, similar in flavour to Black Spanish Round but tapered like a parsnip.

reserves.name: Rudolph
reserves.text: Round red radish for quick early sowings.

reserves.name: Prinz Rotin
reserves.text: Round, red summer radish. Stays crisp and mild when growth is rapid.

reserves.name: Helro
reserves.text: Round, red roots. Grow outdoors in spring and summer, or under cover in winter.

reserves.name: Pink Beauty
reserves.text: Round, pink roots. Adds colour to salads.

reserves.name: Crystal Ball
reserves.text: Globular, all-red. Sow under glass or outdoors from early March onwards.

reserves.name: Sparkler 3
reserves.text: Named red-and-white Sparkler selection sold for summer salads. Harvest young for crisp, mild roots.

reserves.name: Minowase Summer
reserves.text: Summer Japanese-type radish. Sow in May; begin pulling roots at about 6 in. long. Roots can reach about 12 in.

reserves.name: April Cross
reserves.text: Mooli or Japanese radish; matures by autumn from spring sowing.

reserves.name: Minowase
reserves.text: Long white daikon (mooli) radish for raw or cooked dishes. Sow in summer according to the seed packet and protect against cabbage root fly.

reserves.name: Mino Early
reserves.text: White cylindrical roots up to about 12 in. long, with a milder flavour than many winter radishes.

varieties.name: Timperley Early
varieties.text: Early pink-and-green stems; also good for forcing to start the season.

varieties.name: Victoria
varieties.text: Established main-season crop of substantial green-red stalks for pies and preserves.

varieties.name: Raspberry Red
varieties.text: Tender, flavoursome red stalks. Buy named crowns/plants for consistency.

varieties.name: Glaskin's Perpetual
varieties.text: Traditional, economical seed-raised rhubarb; expect variation between plants.

varieties.name: Fulton's Strawberry Surprise

varieties.name: Stockbridge Arrow

reserves.name: Champagne Early
reserves.text: An early red-stemmed rhubarb. Check the supplier’s named selection, as different Champagne cultivars are sold.

varieties.name: Mammoth-Sandwich Island
varieties.text: A white-skinned salsify grown for long roots with a mild flavour. Sold under several Mammoth and Sandwich Island names.

varieties.name: Long Black Maxima (scorzonera)
varieties.text: A scorzonera with long, black-skinned roots and pale flesh. A distinct crop from white-rooted salsify.

varieties.name: Duplex (scorzonera)
varieties.text: A productive scorzonera with long, dark-skinned roots and a delicate flavour.

varieties.name: Duplex (scorzonera)

reserves.name: Giant
reserves.text: Unconfirmed salsify selection: check the supplier’s full name and species. Equivalence to other Mammoth or Giant selections has not been established.

reserves.name: Russian Giant
reserves.text: A black-rooted scorzonera selection. Long Black is another named selection; do not assume the names are interchangeable.

reserves.name: True salsify / vegetable oyster
reserves.text: Cream-coloured roots, grown mainly for their long delicate roots and oyster-like flavour. Leaves are also edible but secondary.

reserves.name: Spanish salsify / scolymus
reserves.text: Golden thistle, Scolymus hispanicus, is a separate edible-root species with spiny foliage. It needs its own cultivation guidance; the salsify spacing and captions here do not describe it.

reserves.name: Scorzonera / black salsify
reserves.text: Black-skinned roots from a perennial plant, also known as Scorzonera hispanica. Sow in spring, commonly March–April; follow the named variety’s packet for depth and spacing. Roots can grow on into a second year.

varieties.name: Medania
varieties.text: Familiar true spinach with generous green leaves for salads or cooking.

varieties.name: Matador
varieties.text: Slow-bolting, deep-green, succulent leaves. Sow small batches for a steady supply.

varieties.name: Monterey F1
varieties.text: Quick hybrid with dark leaves and downy-mildew resistance. Suits warm-season outdoor and protected winter crops.

varieties.name: Giant Winter
varieties.text: Hardy, large-leaved spinach for cooler seasons, complementing spring/early-summer crops.

varieties.name: New Zealand spinach
varieties.text: Heat-tolerant but frost-tender; a spreading summer alternative. Cook the tender shoots in water and discard the water.

varieties.name: New Zealand spinach
varieties.text: Heat-tolerant but frost-tender; a spreading summer alternative. Cook the tender shoots in water and discard the water.

reserves.name: King of Denmark
reserves.text: A traditional spinach with broad, rounded leaves; also valued for slow bolting. Sow in a suitable season and keep watered.

reserves.name: Bloomsdale
reserves.text: Deep green variety which has earned a good reputation for resistance to bolting. Certainly worth a trial.

reserves.name: Long-Standing Round
reserves.text: Popular variety, highly recommended for early spring sowing. Noted for flavour, but late-sown crops may quickly run to seed.

reserves.name: Sigmaleaf
reserves.text: A smooth-seeded spinach suitable for several sowing seasons, including autumn and overwintering. Follow packet dates and keep moisture steady.

reserves.name: Symphony
reserves.text: An F1 spinach with upright growth and large leaves. Check the supplier’s sowing window and named mildew-resistance information.

reserves.name: Space
reserves.text: An F1 spinach with smooth leaves. Choose sowing dates from the seed packet; keep plants cool and evenly watered.

reserves.name: Norvak
reserves.text: A spinach selection retained for its summer and cool-season uses. Follow the supplier’s sowing dates; do not infer the season from seed shape.

reserves.name: Broad-Leaved Prickly
reserves.text: The name refers to the seeds, not the leaves. A standard winter variety; the foliage is dark and fleshy and plants are slow to bolt.

reserves.name: Long-Standing Prickly
reserves.text: Quick to grow and slow to run to seed; old favourite still appearing in catalogues.

reserves.name: Dominant
reserves.text: One of the old favourites, now being replaced in catalogues by newer varieties. Good resistance to bolting.

reserves.name: Monnopa
reserves.text: A smooth-leaved spinach with mild, sweet flavour, described by seed producers as relatively low in oxalic acid. Follow the supplier’s sowing window.

reserves.name: new_zealand_variety
reserves.text: New Zealand spinach (Tetragonia) is a separate Aizoaceae plant. Grow it after frost danger in warm weather; soak seed for 24 hours, sow three per station and thin to one. Pinch tender shoots regularly. It contains oxalates: cook in water and discard that water. Shade from extreme heat if needed.

varieties.name: Crown Prince F1
varieties.text: Blue-grey winter squash with rich orange flesh. Stores well for roasting and winter meals.

varieties.name: Uchiki Kuri
varieties.text: Red-orange winter squash with manageable fruits and rich flesh for cooking and autumn storage.

varieties.name: Hunter F1
varieties.text: Pale-tan butternut with orange flesh for autumn harvests and winter meals.

varieties.name: Sweet Dumpling
varieties.text: Small, striped winter squash for individual portions, alongside larger storage types.

varieties.name: Jack O'Lantern
varieties.text: Orange pumpkin mainly for Halloween carving. Give trailing stems room.

reserves.name: Little Gem
reserves.text: Small round green ball squash which matures quickly to a sweeter flavour and harder skin, like a summer-harvested winter squash.

reserves.name: Musquée de Provence
reserves.text: Large, handsome and often sweet, but needs warmth and a long season.

reserves.name: Marina di Chioggia
reserves.text: Warty green Italian squash with distinctive appearance and good flavour.

reserves.name: Turks Turban
reserves.text: Strikingly shaped and true to its name; useful ornamental and edible squash.

reserves.name: Vegetable Spaghetti
reserves.text: Usually harvested mature for its spaghetti-like cooked flesh. Bake or boil, then loosen the strands; young fruit can also be used as summer squash.

reserves.name: Atlantic Giant
reserves.text: Huge pumpkin requiring a lot of space; grown for size rather than best eating quality.

reserves.name: Summer Crookneck
reserves.text: Long curved fruits with excellent flavour when picked small; larger fruits become creamier and less watery than marrows.

reserves.name: Custard White
reserves.text: A white patty-pan squash with scalloped edges. Pick small and tender for salads or cooking.

reserves.name: Sunspot
reserves.text: Small orange winter squash, similar in use to Uchiki Kuri.

reserves.name: Hungarian Blue
reserves.text: Large blue winter squash, potentially sweet but later than small orange types.

reserves.name: Blue Ballet
reserves.text: Blue-skinned winter squash with good colour and flavour.

reserves.name: Blue Hubbard
reserves.text: Large blue squash with good flavour but a long season.

reserves.name: Hundredweight / Mammoth
reserves.text: A traditional large pumpkin also sold as Mammoth. Allow generous space and grow for size or display.

reserves.name: Butternut
reserves.text: A squash type with tan skins and orange flesh when ripe. Choose an early variety for cooler gardens and allow a full season; sound, fully ripe fruit stores best.

varieties.name: Magres
varieties.text: A purple-topped swede with yellow flesh and good eating quality. A strong addition for an autumn and winter root crop.

varieties.name: Marian
varieties.text: A familiar purple-topped swede with pale yellow flesh.

varieties.name: Tweed F1
varieties.text: A vigorous British-bred hybrid with clubroot resistance. Useful where that disease is a concern, alongside good rotation and soil care.

varieties.name: Joan
varieties.text: Good-flavoured roots for autumn cropping. Sow in late spring or early summer.

varieties.name: Best of All
varieties.text: A hardy, reliable swede with purple skin and yellow flesh.

varieties.name: Ruby
varieties.text: Sweet, yellow-fleshed roots with purple skin. Winter-hardy, with resistance to powdery mildew.

reserves.name: Western Perfection
reserves.text: Reputation based on quick-growing nature. Roots will be ready for lifting in September. Purple-topped roots have yellow flesh.

reserves.name: Acme
reserves.text: Another purple-topped variety which is quick growing like Western Perfection.

varieties.text: Early, compact corn with tender, sweet kernels for short UK summers.

reserves.name: Earliking
reserves.text: Medium-height variety with large cobs. An early variety with a good reputation for sweetness.

reserves.name: First of All
reserves.text: An early traditional sweet corn with medium-sized cobs, around 6 in. long. Choose sowing dates and harvest timing for local warmth.

reserves.name: Kelvedon Glory
reserves.text: A mid-season selection with pale yellow kernels and cobs around 7–8 in. long. Keep watered as cobs fill.

reserves.name: Sundance
reserves.text: An early F1 sweet corn with yellow kernels. Grow in a block and pick at the milky stage.

reserves.name: Earlibelle
reserves.text: Early-maturing variety; cobs are long and well-filled. Stands up well to poor weather conditions.

reserves.name: Dickson
reserves.text: A tall supersweet selection, around 6 ft or more, with cobs up to about 8 in. long.

reserves.name: Sweet 77
reserves.text: Midseason type with very large cobs. Yields and vigour are only moderate.

reserves.name: Candle
reserves.text: A supersweet selection with long, substantial cobs. Allow the full growing season stated by the supplier; maturity depends on local warmth.

reserves.name: Conquest
reserves.text: An early supersweet selection with cobs around 7–8 in. long. Protect young plants from cold checks.

reserves.name: Early Xtra Sweet F1
reserves.text: An early supersweet hybrid, also sold with the spelling Early Extra Sweet. Give warm soil, steady water and the usual full-cob block spacing.

reserves.name: Sweet Nugget F1
reserves.text: A supersweet hybrid with yellow cobs, useful fresh and retaining sweetness after picking. Give a warm site and normal full-cob block spacing.

reserves.name: Minor
reserves.text: A baby-corn selection; pick tender young cobs and eat them whole. Check the supplier’s full selection name.

varieties.name: Sungold F1
varieties.text: A vigorous cordon tomato with very sweet orange cherry fruits. A strong first choice for greenhouse snacking and salads.

varieties.name: Alicante
varieties.text: A traditional red salad tomato grown as a cordon. Retain as an accessible, general-purpose greenhouse variety.

varieties.name: Shirley
varieties.text: An early cordon tomato producing medium red fruits under glass. A familiar, practical choice for an unheated greenhouse.

varieties.name: Sweet Million F1
varieties.text: A cordon with many small red cherry fruits: a red-fruited alternative to orange Sungold.

varieties.name: San Marzano

varieties.name: Red Alert

reserves.name: Moneymaker
reserves.text: A traditional cordon with large trusses of medium-sized red salad tomatoes and good cropping potential.

reserves.name: Ailsa Craig
reserves.text: Another popular variety, producing brightly coloured, medium-sized tomatoes. It matures early but its main claim to fame is excellent flavour.

reserves.name: Harbinger
reserves.text: A traditional early red salad tomato, retained as a distinct variety.

reserves.name: Golden Sunrise
reserves.text: Usual choice for the gardener who wants a yellow tomato. Fruit is medium-sized with a distinctive taste.

reserves.name: Tigerella
reserves.text: Oddity: early-maturing tomato bearing red and yellow stripes when mature. Flavour is good and so is yield.

reserves.name: Apero F1
reserves.text: A small red-fruited cordon with good flavour. Sow in late February–March for greenhouse growing and use normal cordon spacing.

reserves.name: Gardener's Delight
reserves.text: A red cherry cordon with sweet, bite-sized fruits borne in trusses. Suitable under cover or in a warm outdoor site.

reserves.name: Moneycross
reserves.text: A red salad tomato related to Moneymaker. Check current supplier information for its growth habit and any specific disease-resistance claim.

reserves.name: Craigella
reserves.text: A red salad tomato developed from Ailsa Craig, with good flavour. Check the named strain’s disease-resistance information.

reserves.name: Eurocross
reserves.text: A greenhouse hybrid bearing substantial red fruit. Check current supplier guidance for the appropriate greenhouse regime and disease-resistance codes.

reserves.name: Supercross
reserves.text: A Moneymaker-type hybrid with medium-sized red fruit; retained as a distinct selection.

reserves.name: Estrella
reserves.text: A greenhouse hybrid retained as a distinct selection. Check current supplier information for the specific disease-resistance traits.

reserves.name: Grenadier
reserves.text: A productive red salad hybrid with fairly large fruit and useful keeping qualities.

reserves.name: Herald
reserves.text: An early red salad hybrid valued for flavour; retained as its own selection.

reserves.name: Cherry Belle
reserves.text: A productive cherry hybrid with small red fruits and good flavour.

reserves.name: Dani
reserves.text: A productive red tomato hybrid suitable for unheated greenhouse growing.

reserves.name: Typhoon
reserves.text: A vigorous, early hybrid with good cropping potential and red salad fruit.

reserves.name: Big Boy
reserves.text: A large-fruited tomato, sometimes reaching about 1 lb per fruit in good conditions. Allow warmth and space for the crop to ripen.

reserves.name: Dombito
reserves.text: A distinct beefsteak hybrid with thick, fleshy fruit, around ¾ lb in favourable conditions. Allow warmth and support heavy trusses.

reserves.name: Dombello
reserves.text: A separate beefsteak hybrid from Dombito, with large, slightly flattened fruit and good flavour.

reserves.name: Super Marmande
reserves.text: Large, ribbed, meaty red fruit for slicing and cooking. Suppliers describe different training habits: follow the packet for the named strain rather than automatically stopping it at three trusses.

reserves.name: Golden Boy
reserves.text: Variety for a very large yellow fruit which is somewhat juicy.

reserves.name: Yellow Perfection
reserves.text: Yellow tomato reputed to be earlier and sweeter than the others listed.

reserves.name: Rosada F1
reserves.text: A red cherry-plum cordon valued for flavour. Provide support and normal cordon spacing; keep watering steady.

reserves.name: Tumbler F1
reserves.text: Can be grown in a pot on the patio or in a hanging basket with lobelias. Cherry-sized fruits are borne on pendent stems.

reserves.name: Marglobe
reserves.text: A semi-determinate heritage tomato with dense foliage and rounded red fruit. A separate variety from Marmande; support stems as needed.

varieties.name: Outdoor Girl
varieties.text: An early cordon tomato suited to outdoor growing. Provide support and remove sideshoots as for other cordon varieties.

varieties.name: Gardener's Delight
varieties.text: A familiar cordon tomato with small red fruits. A useful outdoor choice in a warm, sheltered position.

varieties.name: Crimson Crush F1
varieties.text: A cordon tomato bred for outdoor growing with strong late-blight resistance. Produces large red fruits for slicing and cooking.

varieties.name: Sungold F1

reserves.name: Roma

reserves.name: Country Taste F1
reserves.text: Large beefsteak substitute mentioned for flavour where sufficient warmth is available.

reserves.name: Sweet 100
reserves.text: A cherry cordon producing many small red fruits. Support well and keep root moisture steady.

reserves.name: Saint Pierre
reserves.text: Another large tomato, irregularly shaped and deep red. Flavour is good and yields are high.

reserves.name: Histon Early
reserves.text: Introduced before F1 hybrids appeared. Still grown for its heavy crops of bright red fruits. Size and flavour are good.

reserves.name: Gemini
reserves.text: An early hybrid cordon with medium-sized, sweet red fruit, suitable for a warm outdoor site.

reserves.name: The Amateur
reserves.text: A compact bush tomato, about 18 in. tall, with medium-sized red fruit. Suitable for sheltered beds or containers.

reserves.name: Pixie
reserves.text: Plants are small and compact but fruits are small and flavour is good - a favourite with many gardeners.

reserves.name: Signal
reserves.text: Good choice: open growth habit allows the crop to ripen in dull weather. It is noted for earliness and quality.

reserves.name: Tornado
reserves.text: Late to fruit, but stems vigorous, foliage sparse and yields high.

reserves.name: Tiny Tim
reserves.text: A dwarf bush tomato with small red cherry fruit, useful in containers or windowboxes.

reserves.name: Sleaford Abundance
reserves.text: A bush tomato producing plentiful small red fruit. The name is recorded in horticultural trials as Sleaford Abundance.

reserves.name: Alfresco
reserves.text: A distinct bush tomato recorded in horticultural research. Retained separately from other outdoor varieties; check supplier guidance for the named selection.

reserves.name: Sub-Arctic Plenty
reserves.text: An early bush tomato for short growing seasons. It is frost-tender, like other tomatoes; protect from cold and continue to watch for blight.

reserves.name: Tumbler F1
reserves.text: A compact trailing cherry tomato for baskets and containers. Keep watered and feed organically as fruit forms; no routine side-shooting.

reserves.name: Marmande
reserves.text: A ribbed, fleshy beefsteak with relatively few seeds. Commonly sold as semi-determinate; follow the strain’s training guidance and give a warm, sheltered site.

reserves.name: Brandywine
reserves.text: Large beefsteak type; may need more heat than many British outdoor sites can provide.

varieties.name: Purple Top Milan

varieties.name: Golden Ball

reserves.name: Red Globe
reserves.text: Globular, medium-sized roots; the flesh is white and the outside white with a red top.

reserves.name: Primera F1
reserves.text: Quick-growing baby turnip. Allow 4 in. between baby roots, or 6 in. for larger early roots, in rows 9-12 in. apart. Harvest young while tender.

reserves.name: Presto
reserves.text: Grow this one for golf-ball sized roots which are pulled about a month after sowing.

reserves.name: Golden Perfection
reserves.text: Flat variety with tender yellow flesh. You may have to search to find it.

reserves.name: Sprinter

reserves.name: Manchester Market

reserves.name: Champion Green-top Yellow

reserves.name: Green-top White
reserves.text: For spring greens or roots. Mature plants develop large, green-topped roots.

reserveListCaveat: The reserves arrays are mechanically unmatched names after normalising case and punctuation, not a curated recommendation list. Aliases, shortened display names, generic crop types, provisional identities and commercially overlapping names require editorial checking. Catalogue counts do not establish the number of distinct additional cultivars.
